newsitem.title: GREECE: GREEK BANK EMPLOYMENT GREW FASTER THAN PUBLIC SECTOR'S.
newsitem.headline: GREEK BANK EMPLOYMENT GREW FASTER THAN PUBLIC SECTOR'S.

text.p: Employment in the Greek banking sector rose faster on average than employment in the public sector in the first half of the 1990s, the economic research department of Alpha Credit Bank said in its December bulletin.
Annual bank employment rose strongly by 5.3 percent and 4.0 percent in 1994 and 1995 as more smaller Greek and foreign banks entered the industry and new banking products were introduced.
Finance and banking sector employment in the United States, United Kingdom, France, Spain, Denmark and Finland declined during the same period but stabilised in Japan, it added.
Greek commercial banks accounted for 82 percent of total employment, specialised credit institutions for 12.5 percent and branches of foreign banks for 5.5 percent, the bulletin added.
Private Ergo Bank and Alpha Credit Bank saw their ratio of employees per branch fall and their market share as a percent of assets rise in the last few years.
But state National Bank , Commercial Bank and Ionian Bank bucked the trend, it said.
National Bank of Greece, the largest commercial bank in the country, employs 32 percent of all bank employees in Greece.

Private Alpha Credit Bank and Ergo Bank also had the highest after-tax profits per worker in the period 1990-1995 and the salaries of their employees grew by the same rate as those of the other three state banks, National, Commercial and Ionian, it added.
Commercial Bank has the highest average employee age among all large banks, driving up the average salary.
National and Commercial had the highest average ratio of personnel to operating expenses during the period 1993-95, the research department of Alpha Credit Bank said.
